impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting judgment as a matter of law that Teva's headache patents claiming humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies for treating headache were invalid for failure to satisfy the written-description and enablement requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 112.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's JMOL of invalidity for Teva's headache patents, reinstating a jury verdict that found Eli Lilly willfully infringed the patents and that the claims were not invalid. The patents cover methods of using humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies to treat headaches, relevant to blockbuster migraine drugs. This decision has major implications for the scope of patent protection available for antibody-based therapeutics.
impacts.positiveImplications: Strengthens patent protection for biologic drug innovators by validating broader genus claims for antibody therapeutics, supporting R&D investment in biologics and protecting market exclusivity for branded migraine treatments.
impacts.negativeImplications: Creates barriers for generic and biosimilar competitors seeking to enter the anti-CGRP antibody market, potentially increasing drug costs and limiting competition in the migraine therapeutic space.

impacts.caseName: Ironburg Inventions Ltd. v. Valve Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly applied inter partes review estoppel under 35 U.S.C. § 315(e)(2) to bar Valve from asserting invalidity grounds not raised in its IPR petition, considering the sufficiency of evidence and the risk of hindsight bias.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's application of IPR estoppel against Valve, finding insufficient evidence to estop one invalidity ground and inadequate consideration of hindsight bias for another. The decision clarifies the evidentiary standard for determining what a 'skilled searcher conducting a diligent search reasonably could have been expected to discover' under § 315(e)(2) estoppel analysis.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides accused infringers with greater latitude to assert invalidity defenses in district court litigation that were not raised in IPR petitions, reducing the risk that IPR estoppel will foreclose meritorious invalidity arguments.
impacts.negativeImplications: Weakens patent holders' ability to rely on IPR estoppel to narrow the scope of invalidity challenges in subsequent litigation, potentially increasing litigation costs and uncertainty for patentees.

impacts.caseName: A.L.M. Holding Company v. Zydex Industries Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner that licenses exclusive commercialization rights but retains the right to sue for infringement (which is not rendered illusory) has sufficient constitutional standing to bring a patent infringement suit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal for lack of standing, holding that a patent owner who retains a non-illusory right to sue for infringement maintains sufficient exclusionary rights to satisfy Article III standing, even after granting an exclusive license for manufacturing and commercialization. This decision clarifies standing requirements for patent owners who structure complex licensing agreements.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides clarity and flexibility for patent owners structuring licensing agreements, confirming they can retain standing to enforce patents even after granting broad exclusive licenses, protecting monetization strategies.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers may face enforcement actions from licensors who retain enforcement rights even where they have licensed away most commercialization rights, complicating defense strategies.

impacts.caseName: Insulet Corp. v. EOFlow, Co. Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Insulet's Defend Trade Secrets Act claim was time-barred under the three-year statute of limitations, where Insulet had access to information suggesting misappropriation more than three years before filing suit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's judgment in favor of Insulet on its DTSA trade secret misappropriation claim against EOFlow, holding that the statute of limitations had expired before Insulet brought suit. The court found that Insulet had sufficient information to discover the alleged misappropriation—involving former employees sharing CAD files and technical information about insulin patch pumps—more than three years before filing. This ruling reinforces strict application of the DTSA's limitations period.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides companies accused of trade secret misappropriation with a strong limitations defense when the plaintiff had early access to facts suggesting misappropriation but delayed filing suit.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret owners must act promptly once they have reason to suspect misappropriation or risk losing their DTSA claims entirely; delay in investigation or filing may be fatal to enforcement.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether there was legally sufficient evidence to support the jury's finding that each of the asserted trade secrets was a protectable trade secret under California law, and whether the same analysis affected patent inventorship claims.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the denial of JMOL on trade secret misappropriation claims, finding insufficient evidence that the asserted trade secrets were protectable because the underlying information was generally known. The court also reversed on patent invalidity, reasoning that the purported inventive contributions were the same generally known ideas. The court affirmed liability for trademark counterfeiting. This case highlights the interplay between trade secret protectability and patent inventorship.
impacts.positiveImplications: Reinforces that trade secret plaintiffs must demonstrate with legally sufficient evidence that their claimed secrets are not generally known, protecting defendants from overreaching trade secret claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies relying on trade secret protection must ensure robust documentation that their claimed trade secrets are genuinely novel and not generally known, or risk losing both trade secret and related patent claims.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding Versata's trade secret damages expert and in its determination of damages for trade secret misappropriation and breach of contract related to automotive configuration software.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to reconsider two previously rejected damages models. The court also reversed the district court's breach of contract damages ruling and reinstated the jury's award, while affirming Ford's liability for trade secret misappropriation of automotive configuration software. This decision provides important guidance on appropriate damages methodologies in trade secret cases involving complex enterprise software.
impacts.positiveImplications: Expands the range of permissible damages models in trade secret cases, giving trade secret owners more flexibility to present unjust enrichment and other damages theories to juries.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop software using knowledge gained from licensed third-party products face increased exposure to trade secret damages claims with potentially broader damages theories.

impacts.caseName: Enanta Pharmaceuticals, Inc. v. Pfizer Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a change from 'C2-C12-alkyl' to 'C1-C12-alkyl' in a patent specification constituted correction of an obvious typographical error, entitling the patent to claim priority from the earlier provisional application and avoiding anticipation by Pfizer's disclosure of nirmatrelvir.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity, holding that Enanta's '953 patent was anticipated because it could not claim priority from the earlier provisional application. The court found that the change from C2 to C1 was not an obvious typographical error, meaning Pfizer's intervening public disclosure of nirmatrelvir (the active ingredient in Paxlovid) anticipated Enanta's claims. This decision has significant implications for pharmaceutical patent priority and the treatment of errors in provisional applications.
impacts.positiveImplications: Protects generic and competing drug manufacturers from being blocked by patents that expand their scope beyond what was originally disclosed in provisional applications, supporting market competition.
impacts.negativeImplications: Pharmaceutical companies must exercise extreme precision in drafting provisional applications, as even minor errors in chemical nomenclature can result in loss of priority and patent invalidation.

impacts.caseName: VLSI Technology LLC v. Intel Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly granted summary judgment of noninfringement of a multicore processor patent based on extraterritoriality and rejection of VLSI's doctrine of equivalents theory.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed in part the district court's grant of summary judgment of noninfringement, finding genuine issues of material fact regarding whether Intel's accused activities occurred within the United States for patent infringement purposes. The court also addressed the striking of damages expert theories for inadequate disclosure. The case involves high-value patents related to multicore processor technology and raises important questions about extraterritorial reach of U.S. patent law.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders asserting claims against multinational technology companies benefit from a broader interpretation of domestic infringement, even where some accused activities occur outside the United States.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies with global operations face increased uncertainty about potential U.S. patent infringement liability for activities with international dimensions.

impacts.caseName: Ollnova Technologies Ltd. v. ecobee Technologies ULC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in its jury instruction and verdict form regarding patent eligibility under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether a single infringement question covering all asserted patents on the verdict form warranted a new trial.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the $11.5 million infringement and damages judgments and remanded for a new trial, finding that the verdict form's use of a single infringement question covering all four asserted patents was prejudicial error. The court also remanded for further analysis under Alice step two for the '495 patent. This decision provides important guidance on the proper structuring of patent trial verdict forms and § 101 jury instructions for building automation system patents.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the requirement that juries must separately evaluate infringement for each asserted patent, preventing potential prejudice from bundled verdict questions.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face increased complexity and risk at trial, as courts may require patent-by-patent verdict questions that give juries more opportunities to find non-infringement on individual patents.

impacts.caseName: AGI SureTrack LLC v. Farmers Edge Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents directed to automated systems for capturing, processing, and sharing farming data using passive data collection devices on farming equipment claim patent-ineligible subject matter under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the case was exceptional under 35 U.S.C. § 285.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that AGI's farming data collection and sharing patents were patent-ineligible under § 101 but vacated and remanded the district court's finding that the case was not exceptional, suggesting fees may be warranted. The court found that the claims were directed to the abstract idea of collecting, analyzing, and sharing farming data, with the claimed relay device and GPS receiver being conventional components. This decision extends § 101 ineligibility to agricultural technology patents.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies in the precision agriculture space benefit from reduced risk of patent infringement suits based on broadly claimed data collection and sharing methods, and may recover fees in exceptional cases.
impacts.negativeImplications: AgTech companies seeking to patent automated farming data systems face heightened § 101 eligibility challenges, potentially undermining investment in agricultural technology innovation.

impacts.caseName: Otsuka America Pharmaceutical, Inc. v. Hetero Labs Limited
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly construed the claim terms 'dextromethorphan' and 'quinidine' in a pharmaceutical patent, and whether the court erred in waiving the Rule 65(c) bond requirement for a preliminary injunction pending appeal.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the preliminary injunction preventing Hetero from launching a generic competitor to Nuedexta (used for treating neurological disorders) but vacated the waiver of the Rule 65(c) bond requirement pending appeal. The court upheld the district court's claim construction regarding weight-to-weight ratios of active pharmaceutical ingredients. This ruling maintains branded drug exclusivity while requiring patent holders to post bonds to protect enjoined parties.
impacts.positiveImplications: Branded pharmaceutical companies can secure preliminary injunctions against generic competitors entering the market before patent expiration, preserving market exclusivity during litigation.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic drug companies face injunctive barriers to market entry, and the bond requirement ensures that if the injunction is later found improper, the enjoined party has recourse for damages suffered during the injunction period.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Rule 30(b)(6) deposition testimony from a corporate representative who lacked personal knowledge was admissible at summary judgment to establish the on-sale bar under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. § 102(b), and whether source code constitutes hearsay.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of patent invalidity under the on-sale bar, holding that a 30(b)(6) corporate representative may testify beyond personal knowledge at summary judgment and that computer source code is not hearsay. The court rejected the argument that the on-sale bar should require express disclosure of a device's functionality, confirming that commercial sales of a device embodying all claim limitations trigger the bar regardless of public knowledge of internal functionality.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies defending against patent infringement can rely on corporate representative testimony and source code evidence to establish prior art defenses, even when original witnesses are unavailable.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face broader evidentiary challenges to their patents under the on-sale bar, as courts accept 30(b)(6) testimony from representatives without firsthand knowledge and treat source code as non-hearsay evidence.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents claiming non-uniform constellations for digital communication systems are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated summary judgment of patent eligibility for two of the asserted patents while affirming eligibility for two others, affirmed the denial of JMOL on non-infringement, and affirmed the damages award. The decision provides important guidance on distinguishing between abstract mathematical concepts and patent-eligible technological improvements in communication systems, splitting the analysis across patents with different claim structures.
impacts.positiveImplications: Technology companies implementing communication standards may benefit from narrower patent eligibility for broadly claimed mathematical optimization methods, while patent holders with sufficiently concrete technological claims retain protection.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders in the communications technology space face uncertainty as courts may draw fine distinctions on eligibility between closely related patents, requiring careful claim drafting to survive § 101 challenges.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the PTAB erred in its obviousness determination of a sensor-based logistics patent, where a third party filed IPR petitions on the filing deadline of the party served with the infringement complaint.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the Board's obviousness determination for FedEx's sensor-based logistics patent and remanded for further proceedings, while declining to review the Board's denial of FedEx's motion to terminate the IPR. The case raises significant concerns about third parties filing IPR petitions at the behest of defendants to circumvent the one-year time bar under § 315(b), a practice with important implications for patent enforcement strategy.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners benefit from closer scrutiny of third-party IPR petitions that may be coordinated with litigation defendants to evade statutory time bars, potentially preserving patent validity.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that rely on third-party IPR filings as part of their defense strategy face increased risk that such petitions will be scrutinized for potential abuse of the IPR system.

impacts.caseName: TrackTime, LLC v. Amazon.com Services LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether claim limitations reciting 'executable program code configured to' perform specified functions should be construed as means-plus-function terms under 35 U.S.C. § 112(f) in light of the Federal Circuit's intervening precedent in Dyfan, LLC v. Target Corp.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the district court's indefiniteness ruling for the '978 patent and remanded for reconsideration of whether § 112(f) applies to 'executable program code configured to' limitations, in light of the intervening Dyfan precedent. The court affirmed the jury's finding of invalidity for the '638 patent. This decision signals that software patent claims using 'configured to' language may avoid means-plus-function treatment under evolving precedent.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software patent holders may benefit from a narrower application of means-plus-function treatment for claims using 'executable program code configured to' language, potentially avoiding indefiniteness invalidity.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers in software patent cases face uncertainty as courts reconsider the scope of § 112(f) for software claim limitations, potentially broadening the scope of enforceable software patents.
